slides.title: Build a tested room-schedule screening workflow
slides.subtitle: Meeting B · comparisons, conditionals, loops, functions, boundary tests, and responsible AI audit
slides.teaching: Students open the Week 03 handout and predict the first three boundary results before running any screening code.

outcomes.head: Translate
outcomes.body: Turn a verbal room criterion into explicit Boolean logic.

outcomes.head: Branch
outcomes.body: Use if, elif, and else with bounded evidence messages.

outcomes.head: Scale
outcomes.body: Apply one tested rule to a small list of room records.

outcomes.head: Refactor
outcomes.body: Package the rule as a reusable function with assertions.

slides.teaching: Ask students which outcome most directly prepares them for later data and machine-learning workflows.

items: Verify one criterion at its boundary
Add conditional messages and compound rules
Repeat the rule across a room schedule
Refactor, test, and audit the final function
slides.teaching: Explain that the studio moves from one value to a reusable evidence pipeline.

slides.title: The studio scales one tested rule without changing its meaning

tiers.task: Evaluate 39.9, 40.0, and 40.1 against an 'at least 40.0 m²' criterion.
Screen [35.0, 40.0, 62.5, 44.2, 28.0] and count rooms meeting the criterion.
Apply area-and-daylight logic to (39.9, True), (40.0, True), and (45.0, False).

slides.teaching: Use this as the challenge map for the handout: no student should attempt the hard function-and-record task before demonstrating the easy boundary and medium accumulator checks.

slides.title: Recall the five logic terms used in the studio
rows: chooses a block using a Boolean
slides.callout: Comparison creates evidence; control flow decides what the program does with it.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L7, L8, and L10. Ask students to point to every term in the Week 03 handout before running code. Move fast: elif, list, and dictionary each receive their own vocabulary slide later in the meeting.

slides.title: Build complexity only after the smaller part works

steps.label: ONE VALUE
steps.head: Verify the comparison
steps.body: Test below, equal, and above the threshold.

steps.label: MANY RECORDS
steps.head: Add repetition
steps.body: Trace the loop item and any accumulator.

steps.label: ONE FUNCTION
steps.head: Refactor and retest
steps.body: Preserve behavior while making the rule reusable.

slides.teaching: This sequence prevents students from debugging comparisons, loops, and functions simultaneously.

slides.title: Start with the Boolean boundary
slides.code:
minimum_m2 = 40.0

print(39.9 >= minimum_m2)
print(40.0 >= minimum_m2)
print(40.1 >= minimum_m2)
slides.explainBody: >= includes equality. > would exclude the exact boundary. Write expected results before running and explain which operator matches the stated criterion.
slides.teaching: Students annotate the three cases in their handout before Ctrl+Enter.

slides.title: Studio 1: prove the comparison matches the words
steps: Underline the phrase that determines equality.
Choose the operator and predict three boundary results.
Run the cell and compare with the predictions.
Write one sentence explaining the policy.
slides.teaching: Do not accept 'because Python says so.' The explanation must connect 'at least' to >=.

slides.title: Branch messages should report evidence, not verdicts
slides.explainBody: The output concerns one area criterion. It does not approve or reject the room as architecture. Status text is part of responsible model communication.
slides.teaching: Compare bounded messages with 'approved' and 'bad room.' Ask what evidence each phrase claims.

slides.title: Studio 2: write and test both branches
slides.prompt: Create a two-branch area screening message.
steps: Write the if and else structure with correct indentation.
Test one value that reaches each branch.
Inspect status in Variable Explorer.
Revise any message that overstates the result.
slides.teaching: Students must demonstrate both branches. One successful run is incomplete branch evidence.

slides.title: elif adds a middle case between if and else
slides.definition: elif means "else, if": a second condition that Python tests only when every condition above it turned out False. A conditional can carry as many elif branches as the rule needs, and exactly one branch ever runs.

example.head: elif daylight_pct >= 15:
example.body: Python reaches this line only after daylight_pct >= 25 was already False. The branch therefore means "between 15 and 25" without your writing that range twice. With daylight_pct = 18, this is the branch that runs.

slides.note: Branches are read top to bottom and the FIRST true one wins. Put the most restrictive threshold first, or 30 gets labeled moderate by a looser branch sitting above it.
slides.teaching: Students met if and else in the asynchronous primer; elif is new today, so give it its own slide before the code. Verified live: with the two thresholds reversed, daylight_pct = 30 prints moderate rather than high. Show that defect here so Studio 3 confirms it rather than discovers it.

slides.title: elif separates several evidence ranges
slides.explainBody: The first true branch wins. Reversing the two thresholds would allow a high value to be captured as moderate.
slides.teaching: Students test 10, 15, 24.9, 25, and 30 before altering the branch order.

slides.title: Studio 3: test every range and transition
steps: Write one expected value inside every range.
Add tests immediately below and at both thresholds.
Reverse two branches and observe the defect.
Restore the correct order and explain why it works.
slides.teaching: The deliberate defect makes branch order visible. Students should identify the first-true-branch rule.

slides.title: Commit to an answer before the compound rule runs
slides.code:
area_m2 = 38.0
has_daylight = True

ready = (
    area_m2 >= 40.0
    and has_daylight
)
print(ready)
slides.question: What does this print?
slides.why: 38.0 >= 40.0 is False. Both sides of an and must be True; reading and as or is the usual trap.
slides.teaching: Poll all four options with a show of hands before revealing. A is the common one: students read and as or, or let the True daylight flag outweigh the failing area. C assumes a rule that fails stores nothing. D assumes and needs two comparisons, so a bare Boolean name looks illegal. Verified on the interpreter: this prints False, and the same expression with or prints True.

slides.title: Compound logic combines criteria explicitly
slides.code:
area_m2 = 44.2
has_daylight = True

ready_for_review = (
    area_m2 >= 40.0
    and has_daylight
)
print(ready_for_review)
slides.explainBody: and expresses an all-required policy. Parentheses and a descriptive Boolean name make the rule readable and testable.
slides.teaching: Students predict all four combinations of two Boolean inputs.

slides.title: Studio 4: construct the truth table
slides.prompt: Test every combination of area criterion and daylight flag.
steps: List False/False, False/True, True/False, True/True.
Predict the result of and for each row.
Run four cases and verify.
Explain when or would encode a different policy.
slides.teaching: Require four cases. Compound conditions cannot be trusted after testing only the all-true row.

slides.title: A list holds several values in one ordered name
slides.definition: A list is one name holding several values in order, written inside square brackets and separated by commas. The order stays exactly as written, so a loop can visit every value once, first to last, with nothing skipped or repeated.

example.head: room_areas_m2 = [35.0, 62.5, 44.2]
example.body: One name, three room areas, in schedule order. A loop over this list reads 35.0, then 62.5, then 44.2, and stops. Add a fourth area later and nothing else in the loop has to change.

slides.note: Square brackets [ ] build a list; parentheses ( ) group an expression; quotation marks make text. '35.0, 62.5' in quotes is one string, not two numbers.
slides.teaching: Square-bracket syntax appears here for the first time in the live meeting, so define it on its own slide rather than inside the loop explanation. Verified: print(room_areas_m2) shows [35.0, 62.5, 44.2].

slides.title: Read the loop header one part at a time

parts.label: Loop keyword
parts.body: Repeats the indented block below, once per list item.

parts.label: Loop variable
parts.body: A new name Python creates. Each pass it holds the next item.

parts.label: Draws from
parts.body: Says where the items come from.

parts.label: The list
parts.body: The list must already exist. The loop leaves it unchanged.

parts.label: Colon
parts.body: Indented lines below run once per item.

slides.teaching: Point at each numbered bracket, then read its numbered label. The two names students confuse are area_m2 and room_areas_m2: one is created by the loop, the other must already exist. Verified: this loop over [35.0, 62.5, 44.2] prints 35.0 False, 62.5 True, 44.2 True.

slides.title: A loop applies one rule to several areas
slides.code:
room_areas_m2 = [35.0, 62.5, 44.2]

for area_m2 in room_areas_m2:
    meets = area_m2 >= 40.0
    print(area_m2, meets)
slides.explainHead: Trace one iteration at a time
slides.explainBody: The loop variable receives the next list item. The indented block executes once per room. Output order follows list order.
slides.teaching: Students trace the first two iterations manually before running.

slides.title: Studio 5: screen a five-room list
slides.prompt: Apply the area comparison without copying it five times.
steps: Predict the loop variable sequence.
Print area beside bounded status text.
Add one area exactly at the threshold.
Explain why one loop is safer than five copied rules.
slides.teaching: Look for duplicated threshold values. The rule should appear once inside the loop or function.

slides.title: Commit to a count before the loop runs
slides.question: What does this print?
slides.why: Two of the three areas pass. Tempting: 3, but the count line runs only when the if is True.
slides.teaching: Hands up for each option before revealing. D (3) is the big one: the loop does run three times, but the counting line is indented under the if, so it runs twice. A (0) assumes print outside the loop reports the starting value. B (1) assumes the line sets the count to 1 rather than adding to it. Verified: this prints 2. The next slide rewrites the same line as passing_count += 1.

slides.title: An accumulator counts passing records
slides.explainBody: The count begins once before the loop, changes inside the true branch, and is reported after every record. += adds to the existing value: passing_count += 1 means passing_count = passing_count + 1, written shorter.
slides.teaching: Introduce += here as shorthand for the line students just predicted. Then show two indentation defects: resetting inside the loop and printing before completion.

slides.title: Trace the accumulator: a fully worked example
slides.callout: passing_count changes only inside the True branch. The value after the loop ends is what print(passing_count) reports.
slides.teaching: Model this table on the board before Studio 6. Students should be able to build the same kind of table for their own five-room list before trusting any accumulator output.

slides.title: Studio 6: count and verify the summary
slides.prompt: Count rooms meeting the criterion and prove the result manually.
steps: Create a trace table for item, condition, and count.
Implement the accumulator with correct indentation.
Compare final count with a hand count.
Add an assertion for the expected count.
slides.teaching: Expected value depends on the supplied list. Students should never accept an accumulator without an independent count. Point back to the worked trace table as the model to follow.

slides.title: Read the function header one part at a time

parts.label: Defines it
parts.body: Creates the function. It does not run it yet.

parts.label: Its name
parts.body: One rule, one name. Call it as area_status(44.2).

parts.label: Input needed
parts.body: The caller must supply this value on every call.

parts.label: Default value
parts.body: Used when the caller omits it. 40.0 is a policy choice.

parts.label: Colon
parts.body: The indented lines below are the function body.

slides.teaching: Default arguments are new today, and part 4 is where they land: 40.0 is a policy the caller may override, not a fact about rooms. Verified: area_status(44.2) returns 'meets area criterion' and area_status(44.2, 50.0) returns 'review area'.

slides.title: A function centralizes the screening rule
slides.explainBody: Parameters expose inputs and default policy. return provides status data to the caller. Every room uses the same rule and vocabulary.
slides.teaching: Students identify function name, parameters, default, branches, return values, calls, and output.

slides.title: Studio 7: refactor without changing behavior
slides.prompt: Move the working conditional into a function.
steps: Define a precise function name and parameters.
Return status text instead of printing inside the function.
Call it for below, equal, and above-boundary cases.
Compare new outputs with the earlier branch outputs.
slides.teaching: Refactoring should preserve behavior. Any changed boundary or message requires explanation.

slides.title: Recall assert - now use it to protect a refactor
slides.code:
assert area_status(39.9) == 'review area'
assert area_status(40.0) == 'meets area criterion'
assert area_status(40.1) == 'meets area criterion'

print('boundary tests passed')
slides.explainBody: Recall from Week 2: assert raises an error when its condition is False, so silence means the claim held. Studio 7 just moved the working conditional into area_status. These three lines prove that refactor preserved the boundary behavior.
slides.teaching: Students already know assert's syntax from Week 2; do not re-teach it from scratch. Change >= to > and show which assertion identifies the policy regression introduced by the refactor: the 40.0 line fails first, because equality is exactly what the operator change removed.

slides.title: Studio 8: write a minimal test suite
slides.prompt: Protect the function's boundary and language.
steps: Assert results below, at, and above the minimum.
Add a non-default minimum and expected result.
Deliberately break the operator and read the failure.
Restore the rule and rerun from a clean kernel.
slides.teaching: Students must observe one failing assertion before restoring the correct function.

slides.title: A dictionary stores each value under a name
slides.definition: A dictionary stores values under names instead of positions. You write key: value pairs inside curly braces, then read one value back by putting its key in square brackets. Use it when a record has fields worth naming.

example.head: {'name': 'Lobby', 'area_m2': 35.0}
example.body: Store this record as room. Then room['area_m2'] returns 35.0 and room['name'] returns 'Lobby', read by key rather than by position, so adding another field cannot break the lookup.

slides.note: A list is read by position, a dictionary by key. Both are read with [ ], so say which one you built before you index into it.
slides.teaching: Keep the coverage minimal, as the schedule directs: one record, one lookup, no catalog of dictionary methods. Verified: room = {'name': 'Lobby', 'area_m2': 35.0} then room['area_m2'] returns 35.0 and room['name'] returns 'Lobby'.

slides.title: A real room schedule, not a toy of three
slides.explainBody: Each item in this list is one room's dictionary. room['area_m2'] will hand the tested function one value per room — the studio emphasis stays on control flow and functions, not a catalog of collection methods. Office sits exactly on the 40.0 boundary — predict its status before the next slide reveals it.
slides.teaching: Explain list-of-dictionaries only to the extent needed to read one record and apply the tested function.

slides.title: ...continued: apply the rule to every room
slides.output:
Lobby review area
Studio A meets area criterion
Gallery meets area criterion
Workshop meets area criterion
Seminar review area
Studio B meets area criterion
Office meets area criterion
Storage review area
slides.explainBody: room['area_m2'] hands the tested function one value; the function itself has not changed since cell [7]. Eight rooms, one rule, zero duplicated thresholds.
slides.teaching: Confirm Office (exactly 40.0) landed in 'meets area criterion' — the >= from cell [1] made that call, not a coin flip.

slides.title: ...continued: count the report, don't just print it
slides.code:
review_count = 0
meets_count = 0
for room in rooms:
    status = area_status(room['area_m2'])
    if status == 'review area':
        review_count += 1
    else:
        meets_count += 1
print('Review:', review_count, 'Meets:', meets_count)
assert review_count + meets_count == len(rooms)
print('Every room accounted for')
slides.output:
Review: 3 Meets: 5
Every room accounted for
slides.explainBody: Two counters, updated once per room inside the same loop that already printed the report — nothing new here except reusing what Week 1's accumulator and Week 3's assert already taught. The assertion is the check: if any room's status fell through both branches, the counts would not add up to len(rooms).
slides.teaching: Ask what would need to change in area_status for a room to satisfy NEITHER count — this is exactly why the assertion is worth keeping, not decorative.

slides.title: Studio 9: audit an AI-generated screening rule
slides.prompt: AI excludes equality and labels passing rooms “approved.”
steps: Identify the operator and communication defects.
Repair the function and its status messages.
Add boundary assertions that fail on the original.
Record accepted, modified, and rejected suggestions.
slides.teaching: Require evidence from tests, not merely a claim that the repaired code looks better.

slides.title: Submit a small reproducible evidence package

steps.label: SCRIPT
steps.head: Clean .py workflow
steps.body: Runs from the top in a restarted kernel.

steps.label: OUTPUT
steps.head: Room status report
steps.body: Names each record and bounded result.

slides.teaching: Use peer verification before submission. One student runs while the other checks all four artifacts.

slides.title: One tested rule can scale without losing accountability
takeaways: Exercise every branch and compound condition.
Trace loop state and verify summaries independently.
Centralize policy in a function protected by assertions.
slides.teaching: Students save, restart, run from the top, and submit the script and brief rule limitation.
